name: Glass skin routine

card.summary: A K-beauty goal of poreless, translucent, glowing skin pursued through a multi-step routine; online it is as much an aesthetic ideal as a defined protocol, with no dedicated clinical studies.
card.note: A look and a routine style, not a clinical protocol; individual steps such as sunscreen and acne care are studied separately.

quick.overview:
Glass skin refers to a look of smooth, even, luminous skin that appears almost translucent, popularised through Korean skincare and social media. The associated routine layers many products such as oil and water cleansers, exfoliation, essences, ampoules, moisturiser and sunscreen.

On looksmax.org, users discuss it as both a goal and a routine, with posters debating how much depends on genetics versus diet and skincare. No published study evaluates the glass skin routine itself.
quick.mechanism: Posters describe a layered routine: double cleansing, gentle chemical exfoliation (BHA/AHA) about once a week, hydrating essences or ampoules, moisturiser and daily sunscreen, plus diet and hydration. The visual effect is attributed to hydration, even texture and reduced inflammation.
quick.risks: Overuse of exfoliating acids is a commonly discussed irritation risk, which some posters themselves caution against. Forum posts mix routine advice with dietary claims and talk of prescription acne drugs, which are outside the routine itself.

lead: Glass skin is a skincare goal from Korean beauty culture: skin that looks smooth, even, pore-minimal and faintly translucent, with a dewy sheen. People pursue it with a layered routine of cleansing, gentle exfoliation, hydrating essences or ampoules, moisturiser and daily sunscreen, aiming for a clearer, more luminous complexion that reads as healthy and youthful in person and in photos.[1]

Wikipedia describes the look as favoured in South Korea and achieved less through foundation than through a long skincare routine, averaging around ten steps, that starts with a double cleanse and moves through sheet masks, essences, serums and moisturiser to SPF sunscreen by day.[1] The term spread through social media, and on looksmax.org it appears both as a trend and as a routine people try to follow for acne and texture.[3][4]

No clinical study has tested a glass skin routine as a whole. Its individual parts, such as moisturiser, sunscreen, cleansing and exfoliation, are covered in general skin care references, which also note that over-exfoliation can cause irritation and barrier damage.[5]
infobox: Double cleanse, exfoliation, essence, ampoule, moisturiser, sunscreen

paras: Wikipedia's K-beauty article describes a routine that begins with a double cleanse, continues through sheet masks, essences, lotions, serums and rich moisturisers, and ends with SPF sunscreen in the daytime or a thicker sleep cream at night.[1] A representative looksmax.org guide lists an oil-based cleanser, then a water-based cleanser, a BHA or AHA exfoliant about once a week, a moisturising essence, an ampoule, moisturiser and sunscreen, with a food list and advice to drink plenty of water.[3] Another poster describes a simpler acne-focused version: a foaming cleanser, a chemical exfoliant, avoiding physical scrubs while acne is active, plus diet and water changes.[4]

Korean beauty traces its roots to the Three Kingdoms period, with the Goryeo era regarded as a peak, and reached Western markets in 2011 with the BB cream, according to Wikipedia.[1] Asia-Pacific held the largest market share as of 2020, and the Korean Wave of dramas and music has been credited with driving sales.[1] Glass skin spread globally through social media as a visual shorthand for the whole routine.

sections.h: Components and general skin care background
paras: General skin care references describe cleansers as removing oil, dirt and makeup with surfactants, with synthetic detergent cleansers milder than traditional alkaline soap.[5] Moisturisers raise skin water content through humectants, occlusives and emollients, and sunscreen shields skin from UV damage that causes sunburn and premature aging.[5]

Chemical exfoliants are described as generally gentler than mechanical scrubs, but excessive exfoliation can cause irritation and barrier damage, and people with inflammatory acne are advised to exfoliate cautiously.[5]

Forum threads on glass skin range from routine guides to before-and-after acne accounts.[3][4] One poster asked whether anyone had reached the look through lifestyle and skincare alone, suggesting people who have it often already had a good genetic base; a reply credited the product centella for the glassy finish.[6] A Lemmy skincare thread shows the same interest outside looksmaxxing, from a woman in her forties asking how to get the glassy look.[7]
No studies found. The routine's individual components, such as sunscreen, retinoids or acne treatment, are studied separately in the dermatology literature but not as a glass skin protocol.

lore.intro: Glass skin is discussed on looksmax.org as both a K-beauty trend and a skincare goal, with threads giving routines and personal before-and-after accounts.[3][4][6]

claims.claim: Glass skin is achievable through a layered K-beauty routine.
claims.believers: Posters publish step lists of oil and water cleansing, weekly exfoliation, essence, ampoule and sunscreen, and one reports going from severe oily acne to clear skin over about six months with a cleanser, chemical exfoliant and diet changes.[3][4]
claims.experts: No published study has tested the glass skin routine as a whole; individual steps are evaluated separately in dermatology.[5]

claims.claim: Specific foods and heavy water intake produce clearer, glassy skin.
claims.believers: A forum guide lists foods such as walnuts, avocado and tomatoes as helpful, and advises avoiding fried food, sugar, cheese and coffee, while another thread recommends several litres of water daily.[3][4]
claims.experts: No published studies were found linking the foods or water volumes in these posts to a glass skin look.

claims.claim: The glass look depends largely on genetics, with routine changing one or two things
claims.believers: One poster argues people with the look usually had a strong genetic base and only needed to stop habits such as sugar binging.[6]
claims.experts: No published study has examined how much of the glass skin appearance is attributable to genetics versus routine.

angle.text: The routine aims at hydrated, calm, evenly textured skin that reflects light, which people describe as the glass look. Followers attribute the result to consistency with cleansing, hydration, gentle exfoliation and sunscreen.
